# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has drastically altered the treatment of obstructive coronary artery disease. However, the progressive shift from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and permanent drug-eluting stents (DES) was long hindered by the persistent presence of a metallic cage. This permanent implant impairs vasomotion, induces chronic local inflammation, leads to late lumen loss, and limits future coronary artery bypass grafting options, exposing patients to a lifelong risk of late-term adverse events. To overcome these limitations, the paradigm of "vascular restorative therapy" was proposed through the development of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) [1,2]. These temporary devices are designed to provide transient mechanical support and local drug delivery to prevent early recoil and restenosis, and subsequently undergo gradual bioresorption, ideally restoring vasomotor function and local vessel geometry [2,3,4].

The pioneer in this field was the Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular), which featured a poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) backbone [1,5]. Early clinical evaluations in the ABSORB Cohort A and Cohort B trials demonstrated the feasibility of BVS, showing progressive scaffold resorption and restoration of vasomotor response at long-term follow-up [1,2,3,4]. Multi-modality imaging investigations, including optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound, showed favorable neointimal healing and scaffold degradation [3,4]. This success led to larger-scale clinical evaluation, including the ABSORB II randomized trial [5] and the pivotal ABSORB III trial [6]. Further global clinical validation followed in the ABSORB Japan trial [7] and the ABSORB EXTEND registry [8].

Despite this early promise, larger clinical datasets raised serious safety concerns. Pooled analyses [9] and long-term results of major trials—including the 3-year outcomes of ABSORB II [10] and ABSORB III [11]—revealed a significant increase in adverse clinical events compared to metallic DES. This was further highlighted by the independent AIDA trial [12], which reported higher rates of device thrombosis, and the large-scale ABSORB IV trial [13]. Large systematic reviews and meta-analyses [14,15,16] confirmed that BVS carried a twofold to threefold higher risk of both target lesion failure (TLF) and scaffold thrombosis (ST), particularly very late scaffold thrombosis [17]. High-risk clinical scenarios, such as ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) [18,19], as well as real-world registries like the Italian GISE registry [20], consistently documented elevated rates of device failure.

Investigating the mechanisms of BVS failure revealed key physical and procedural elements. The thick struts of first-generation PLLA scaffolds (~150 µm) altered local fluid dynamics, caused shear-stress alterations, and delayed endothelialization [21]. Structural disruption, poor expansion, and the mechanics of PLLA degradation (causing late strut discontinuity) also contributed to late events [21,22]. This emphasized the critical role of implantation technique. An expert consensus recommended the "PSP" protocol: meticulous Pre-dilation, accurate vessel Sizing, and high-pressure Post-dilation [22]. Although optimizing technique improved outcomes, safety concerns prompted professional societies like the European Society of Cardiology to issue cautionary statements [23], and the 2018 ESC/EACTS Guidelines downgraded BVS use to clinical registries only [24].

These experiences prompted the development of next-generation bioresorbable scaffolds with thinner struts and alternative materials. Highly promising among these are magnesium-based resorbable scaffolds, studied in the BIOSOLVE-I [25] and BIOSOLVE-II trials [26], as well as the DREAMS-2G registry [27], which demonstrated excellent safety and fast degradation (resorption within 12 months) [28]. Polycarbonate-based scaffolds with radiopacity, such as the Fantom scaffold [29], and long-term real-world trials of magnesium scaffolds like BIOSOLVE-IV [30] represent major advances.

In conclusion, while the initial clinical introduction of first-generation BVS was marred by elevated rates of scaffold thrombosis, it provided invaluable insights into vascular biology, lesion preparation, and device design. The paradigm of vascular restorative therapy remains highly attractive. Ongoing developments focused on thinner-strut PLLA, iron-based, and magnesium-based scaffolds hold promise to safely realize the long-term benefits of a temporary vascular implant.
